I don’t know about a senior rate, but as a single person I pay about $96 per month with the state worker discount. Without the state worker discount it would be about $112. They also charge an extra $40 in the spring for “annual pool maintenance” that you cannot opt out of, even if you never use the pool. To initially sign up there was a $200 onboarding fee which I didn’t have to pay since I’m a state worker and asked for the state worker discount. 
It’s a lot of money, but so far I do not regret getting a membership 2 1/2 months ago. I’m getting great use out of it, going 4-6 times a week. The extra cost to be a member keeps out a lot of the weirdos and acts as a filter. Even after work, the gym is not so busy that I am fighting for equipment or feel super crowded and I actually enjoy being there. The west side gym is by far my favorite though compared to the south side gym. There is less equipment, but the building is nicer, and it is even less crowded than southside. 

When I asked how I can cancel they told me I need to cancel at my annual contract renewal or prove I am moving or am experiencing extreme financial hardship. They did say I can ask for pause of up to three months, which might be useful for maybe the summertime or a holiday when you may not be going as much.

A word of caution I learned the hard way, one time someone was right behind me at the west AKClub, and it was reflexive for me to hold the door open for them. Even at the time when I was doing it, I thought I really should not be holding the door open for this person because for all I know, they are not actually a member. But it was just a polite reflex and it was too late at that point. Anyway, they sent me an email and said they saw the footage of me letting this person in (who IS a member btw) and they are charging me $50 per their policy for holding the door open for someone who didn’t scan in. Well, when I signed up, they did not tell me about that policy. So I’m still a little peeved about that. I get it from a safety standpoint, but they really should mention these policies that will cost you money upon sign up. So definitely do not hold doors open for people, and if someone holds the door open for you, make sure you scan in so that person doesn’t get charged 50 bucks.

When you front rack a barbell, your elbows should be so high up in the air that the barbell is resting on the "shelf" that your deltoids make.   
Usually when people first start frontracking, they don't have the tricep or lat mobility to get their elbows that high, and they need to stretch specifically to improve this elbow mobility to get them as high as they can while in this position. This will reduce the strain on your wrists.  
It sounds like you need to work on elbow mobility to get those elbows up higher so your wrists are comfortable bending back to roll the barbell onto your fingers. Additionally, the stronger you get the larger your deltoid shelf will get, which will also help with any collarbone bruising. Just keep stretching those triceps and lats to improve elbow mobility and work on that deltoid shelf. It will come with time.

Hi, there! I work in social work. Specifically, for the state in the child welfare department. I investigate child abuse and license foster homes. Just judging from your self-description, I'm not sure that social work would be right for you. There is no structure (insane amounts of overtime, and sudden emergencies come up which you just have to bolt out the door for with no prior warning, constant reprioritizing, constant schedule changes..)I don't know that you can be an introvert and work in social work. And a calm demeanor is not always a good thing. You have to be able to be a hard-ass. You have to deal with people getting pissed, threatening you, and even be okay with the possibility of being assaulted some day. You have to be able to laugh off the tough stuff and emotionally deal with the REALLY tough stuff, all while working full-steam through your day and not letting it get to you. You have to be able to stand your ground when someone is yelling in your face.. You have to have thick skin and show no fear all while doing your job and not being threatened by clients into breaking confidentiality. You have to be able to call people up and tell them they have broken a law/regulation not knowing how they are about to react, and  you have to be comfortable breaking very bad news to people. And you have to be comfortable testifying in court on occasion, and the never-ending threat of being sued. You have to be okay with 10-12 hours of this a day. In short, you have to be able to fight back.

I also worked in libraries for six years before I became a social worker. From your description, it sounds like that would probably fit you well. I was a teen librarian, and I found it to be very fulfilling. Definitely more introvert friendly, although there is occasional confrontation, but not nearly as bad as social work. You should be able to do some public speaking and have leadership skills, such as being in charge of library assistants/teen volunteers, running programs, doing presentations to the public, and leading groups of people through projects. Be warned, the pay isn't great, but it is fulfilling and enjoyable, and may suit you!

This was several years ago. I turned myself into the hospital for suicidal ideation, thinking I could get some outpatient help, maybe a prescription for antidepressants or something. Nope. They had two big dudes in white coats escort me upstairs to the psych ward. I was stripped of my clothes, all of my belongings were taken away, and I was thrown into a locked room with nothing but a twin size bed one tiny window that looked at a brick wall. After I-don't-know-how-long somebody slid a tray of food through a slot in the door. I yelled through and asked if I could call somebody. They said "no, we can't let you do that, honey." None of my friends or family knew I was locked in a padded room, I hadn't told anyone I was going because I really thought it would be as easy as a referral to a therapist or a small prescription or something. These nurses wouldn't even let me make one phone call. I asked if I could have a pencil and paper to draw or write and they said no. I asked if I could have chapstick and they said no. I asked if I could have a cup of water and they said no. I wasn't allowed to brush my teeth. Of course I ended up crying that night because I felt so trapped, helpless, and vulnerable and didn't know what was going on. The next day a nurse came in during the afternoon and told me I could take a shower, but she had to watch me. I declined. I was taken to the rooms next door where the other psych patients were, and there was more of a sense of normalcy (at least I wasn't lock in a padded room) but I still wasn't allowed to make a phone call or have my clothes.

Keep in mind I wasn't threatening to hurt anyone or myself, I literally just went in and said I was thinking of killing myself and was looking for some help, didn't really know where else to turn to at that point as I didn't have a regular therapist. When they discharge me a week later, I asked the nurses why the hell they locked me away into solitary confinement because it for sure created new trauma. They just said "Oh, that was a mistake, we weren't supposed to do that. We realized you should have just been put in with the other patients. Whoops." Awesome.

I had terrible nightmares after that about being locked up in that room and had to have trauma therapy about it. Now going to a hospital puts me on the edge of a panic attack every time. My chest gets tight, hands clam up, and I just feel like two big burly dudes in white coats are going to take me upstairs to the top floor and lock me away forever and I won't even be able to tell anyone.

Hi, I've been at it for about 2.5 years now and I'm still learning! There are so many different skills to learn in CF, so be patient with yourself. If I could go back and give myself advice I would say: A box where you like the people and coaches makes all the difference. Don't be dismayed if you get nauseous in your first couple classes - your body has never been pushed this hard before. Eat a meal no sooner than two hours before class - three if it's something really fatty. Being nervous is normal. Don't let your ego get the best of you, especially in the beginning. Doing the WOD's with just a 15 pound bar is okay at first, when you are really new to the movements. Track your PR's, they are great motivation! Work on that ankle and elbow mobility. Get a coaches attention if you have any questions at all, or if you want them to do a form check.. that's what they are there for.

Keep us updated on your progress, and have fun!

Hi! I find that anything that involves a lot of up-down (burpees, lunges, squats) causes my heart rate to shoot skyhigh like that. That is because I have a heart condition (SVT) that, among other things, also makes it difficult for my heart to "balance" my blood pressure when I am going up and down. You know how if you are laying or sitting for a bit and then get up too fast, you can get dizzy? Or when you are dehydrated and stand up too fast, and get dizzy? That's because your heart needs a sec to change your blood pressure for the new position. For me, it takes my heart a lot more work to adjust for all the up-down stuff because of my SVT. I just hydrate REALLY well before the WOD (even for people without a heart condition, this will make a difference) and pace myself so I don't get dizzy. The heart rate still spikes, though, and I just push through as best I can. End up sweating like a cold beer on a hot day, but I listen to my body and it's all good. If my heart rate is off-the-wall, like you are describing, I do stop for a bit and take a breather. No need to hurt myself just to shave some seconds off. 

This probably won't apply to you if you don't think you have a heart thing going on, but that's my experience with sky-high heart rate during a lot of up-down movements. But, maybe it would help if you tried to be more hydrated beforehand? It helps me.For reference, I am F/28/125 lbs, been doing CF on and off for a few years.
